title: Momentum and collisions
note: Momentum p = mv is a vector. Impulse FΔt equals the change in momentum, so spreading a collision over more time lowers the force. When the net external force on a system is zero, its total momentum is conserved in every collision; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones.

read.title: What collisions keep
text: Momentum is mass times velocity, a vector that captures how hard it is to stop something. Newton originally wrote his second law in terms of momentum: the net force equals the rate of change of momentum. Rearranged, the impulse FΔt equals the change in momentum Δp.

That relation explains much of safety engineering. A car stopping in a crash must lose its momentum no matter what. Airbags, crumple zones, and padded dashboards cannot change Δp, but they stretch out Δt, so the average force on the passenger drops.

The real power of momentum is conservation. Inside any system, forces come in third-law pairs that cancel when summed, so internal forces cannot change the total momentum. If the net external force is zero, the momentum before a collision equals the momentum after, whether objects bounce, stick, or explode apart.

Kinetic energy is less reliable. In an elastic collision, such as between hard steel balls, kinetic energy is also conserved. In an inelastic collision some kinetic energy becomes heat, sound, or deformation. When objects stick together the collision is perfectly inelastic and loses the most kinetic energy that momentum conservation allows.

q.q: Why can't internal forces change a system's total momentum?
o: They come in pairs that cancel
